cards.explanation: The answer is a census. The LORD says to David, Israel's king, “Go and take a census of Israel and Judah.” Counting heads sounds like the most harmless chore in the world. But this one has some weight to it, so stay close, friends.

The answer is number. David says he wants Joab to register the troops “…so that I may know their number.” He's after a total, plain and simple. I double-check my cookie boxes before I seal them, but David is trying to count a whole nation's worth.

The answer is False, and Joab is the reason. Joab, the commander of David's army, says, “But why does my lord the king want to do such a thing?” (2 Samuel 24:3). He's the one in the meeting who asks whether we're sure about this. I think everybody needs a Joab around.

The answer is the king's word. The text says, “Nevertheless, the king’s word prevailed against Joab and against the commanders of the army.” (2 Samuel 24:4). Joab and the commanders push back, and it still doesn't change the order. Push all you like, friends, the king's word carries the day.

The answer is nine months and twenty days, right on the nose. The text says, “At the end of nine months and twenty days, having gone through the whole land, they returned to Jerusalem.” (2 Samuel 24:8). That's almost ten months on the road. A batch of cookies takes me one afternoon, so this is a different kind of job.

The answer is True. After the count, “…his conscience was stricken…” and David says to the LORD, “I have sinned greatly in what I have done.” (2 Samuel 24:10). He says it to the LORD himself. Gad hasn't shown up yet at that point.

The answer is foolishly. David says, “Now, O LORD, I beg You to take away the iniquity of Your servant, for I have acted very foolishly.” (2 Samuel 24:10). He doesn't dress it up or pass it along. He puts it plainly to the LORD and asks Him to take it away.

The answer is three options, friends. Gad, David's prophet and seer, brings the LORD's words: “I am offering you three options. Choose one of them, and I will carry it out against you.” (2 Samuel 24:12). David gets to choose, and the LORD will carry out the one he picks. That's a weighty menu.

The answer is that the LORD's mercies are great. David says, “…for His mercies are great; but do not let me fall into the hands of men.” (2 Samuel 24:14). Look at where he puts his hope. He'd rather land in the LORD's hand than anyone else's.

The answer is False. The angel stretches out his hand to destroy Jerusalem, but “…the LORD relented from the calamity…” and said, “Enough! Withdraw your hand now!” (2 Samuel 24:16). The LORD stops him before it happens. I think that's a moment to breathe out.

The answer is by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. The text says, “At that time the angel of the LORD was by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.” (2 Samuel 24:16). Araunah, a Jebusite, owns that threshing floor. Keep that place in mind, friends, because it matters a lot in the next verses.

The answer is that he asks the LORD to let His hand fall on David and his father's house. David says, “Please, let Your hand fall upon me and my father’s house.” (2 Samuel 24:17). The shepherd steps in front of the sheep. I think this one hurts a little to read.

The answer is an altar to the LORD. Gad, David's prophet and seer, says, “Go up and build an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.” (2 Samuel 24:18). The instruction comes that same day, after David speaks to the LORD.

The answer is False. The text says, “So David went up at the word of Gad, just as the LORD had commanded.” (2 Samuel 24:19). The king walks up there himself. Araunah sees “…the king and his servants coming toward him…” (2 Samuel 24:20).

The answer is to buy the threshing floor. David says to Araunah, “To buy your threshing floor… that I may build an altar to the LORD, so that the plague upon the people may be halted.” (2 Samuel 24:21). He says it straight to Araunah's face. No hints, no games.

The answer is True. Araunah gives it all to the king. David answers, “No… I insist on paying a price, for I will not offer to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing.” (2 Samuel 24:24). Then he buys the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.

The answer is nothing. David says, “…I will not offer to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing.” (2 Samuel 24:24). He wants a gift that costs him something. He's not about to hand over a free one.

The answer is fifty shekels of silver. The text says, “So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.” (2 Samuel 24:24). The price is stated plain as day. He pays it, and the altar comes next.

The answer is halted. The text says, “Then the LORD answered the prayers on behalf of the land, and the plague upon Israel was halted.” (2 Samuel 24:25). It stopped. I think that's a long breath out for everybody.
